summary: An Applicability Statement describing how to exchange structured business data, such as XML or EDI, securely using FTP with MIME packaging. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Companies swap orders and invoices as files. This describes sending them over FTP in a packed, signed and secret form so the receiver trusts them.

questions: secure b2b data exchange over ftp
what is a signed mdn receipt
what is the secure transmission loop
subtitle: How trading partners swap signed, encrypted business documents over FTP and get signed receipts back.

tldr.problem: Companies exchanging EDI, XML or other business data over the Internet need privacy, integrity, proof of who sent it and proof that it arrived, but plain FTP offers none of these.
tldr.mechanism: The document is packaged as a MIME message, signed and encrypted with S/MIME, and uploaded by FTP. The receiver checks it and uploads back a message disposition notification (MDN) that can be signed.
tldr.outcome: The RFC calls itself the third applicability statement from the IETF EDIINT working group, hence AS3. It is Informational and is updated by RFC 8996, which is the only later change noted in the metadata.

today: RFC 4823 is Informational and is updated by RFC 8996. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What AS3 Does
sections.content:
This Applicability Statement describes how to exchange structured business data securely using the File Transfer Protocol (FTP). The data can be EDI (ANSI X12 or UN/EDIFACT), XML, binary or anything else for which MIME packaging can be done with standard content types. It builds on RFC 1767 and earlier EDI-over-SMTP work and tries to re-invent as little as possible. The goals are data privacy, integrity, authenticity, non-repudiation of origin and non-repudiation of receipt.

The flow is simple. The sender uploads an appropriately packaged message by FTP. The receiving application polls its FTP server for inbound messages, unpackages them and returns a message disposition acknowledgement, signed or unsigned, inside a multipart/report. Authentication and confidentiality come from S/MIME security body parts.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender leaves a locked, sealed package in a shared folder. The receiver keeps checking the folder, opens the package and leaves a receipt behind.

sections.title: The Secure Transmission Loop and Options
sections.content:
The Secure Transmission Loop (STL) has two steps. The originator sends a document that is signed and encrypted and that asks for a signed receipt. The recipient decrypts the document, verifies the signature and returns a signed receipt, which contains the hash of the signature of the received message. The STL gives integrity, sender authenticity and non-repudiation of receipt, but the RFC does not require it.

Non-repudiation of receipt (NRR) is a legal event that occurs only when the original sender has verified the signed receipt, and it is not possible without signatures. The RFC lists twelve permutations that a trading relationship can use: data unencrypted, encrypted, signed, or encrypted and signed, each with no receipt, an unsigned receipt or a signed receipt. Number 12 is the STL.

For signatures, SHA-1 is RECOMMENDED for outgoing messages, but both MD5 and SHA-1 MUST be supported for incoming messages. Compression is supported through RFC 3274. The EDI interchange, including its envelope segments, is the unit that is signed and encrypted, so the envelope is not visible in the MIME package.
sections.plainLanguage: The best mode is like sending a locked box with a note saying "send me a signed receipt". The receiver opens the box, checks the seal and returns a receipt signed with their own pen, so nobody can later say it never arrived.

sections.title: Message Structure and Headers
sections.content:
An AS3 message is a MIME message with the usual headers plus a few AS3-specific outer headers. Depending on the options it is plain, a multipart/signed, an application/pkcs7-mime encrypted body, or an encrypted signed body. The content types that MUST be supported include multipart/signed, multipart/report, message/disposition-notification, application/PKCS7-signature, application/PKCS7-mime, application/EDI-X12, application/EDIFACT, application/edi-consent and application/XML.

AS3-From and AS3-To identify the sender and receiver and MUST be present in all AS3 messages and MDNs. Each is a case-sensitive name of 1 to 128 printable ASCII characters, such as a DUNS number or any string the partners agree on, and the header MUST NOT be folded. AS3-Version is required only if the value is not 1.0, and 1.1 indicates support for EDIINT data compression.

An AS3 message MUST contain AS3-To, AS3-From, Date, Message-ID and Content-Type. A message requesting a receipt MUST contain Disposition-Notification-To. Content-Transfer-Encoding SHOULD NOT be used, a MIME epilogue SHALL NOT be used, and Message-Id is limited to 998 characters.
sections.plainLanguage: Each package has a label saying who it is from, who it is to, and its own ticket number, so the receipt can say exactly which package it is about.

sections.title: FTP Transport and Receipts
sections.content:
FTP is long viewed as insecure because of cleartext authentication. Conforming AS3 implementations SHALL use FTP clients and servers that support the AUTH command from RFC 2228, and AUTH TLS (from RFC 4217) MUST be supported. AS3 requires the default file structure and the image transfer type.

The receipt is a Message Disposition Notification (MDN) as defined in RFC 3798. It is returned over a separate FTP connection: the sender connects and sends the AS3 message, disconnects, then the receiver connects and sends the MDN. The requester asks for one with a Disposition-notification-to header holding an FTP URL, and asks for a signed receipt by giving signed-receipt-protocol and signed-receipt-micalg options, for example pkcs7-signature with sha1 or md5.

A signed MDN is a multipart/signed message whose first part is the multipart/report and whose second part is the pkcs7 signature. It contains a Received-content-MIC field with the base64 digest of the received content, which the sender compares with its own digest to verify the receipt. The MDN disposition says whether the message was processed, with modifiers such as error: decryption-failed, authentication-failed, integrity-check-failed, insufficient-message-security, decompression-failed or unexpected-processing-error. An implementation MUST present an FTP server interface for inbound documents and MDNs, and MUST be able to send to a partner's FTP server.
sections.plainLanguage: The package goes into the other company's folder. Later the other company puts a receipt, with a fingerprint of the package, into your folder. If the fingerprints match, you know they got the right thing.

sections.title: Certificates and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Partners exchange public keys as part of setting up the trading relationship, and the software keeps a database of those keys together with the mapping from trading partner ID to FTP URL. X.509 certificates are REQUIRED, but a certification authority is OPTIONAL: partners are RECOMMENDED to self-certify each other if they have no agreed authority, and certificates may be self-signed. The complete certification chain MUST be included in all certificates, and all certificate verifications MUST chain to root.

The security section quotes the S/MIME specifications. 40-bit encryption is weak and gives little security over plaintext, and software should warn the user clearly when a certificate cannot be shown to be valid, for example when it is expired, revoked or does not chain to a trusted CA. Section 6.1 also notes that the AUTH TLS reference relies on TLS version 1.0, not 1.1.
sections.plainLanguage: Both companies must swap their official stamps ahead of time. If a stamp looks wrong or expired, the software has to shout about it rather than quietly accept the package.
